newsitem.title: USA: N.J. investment adviser charged in fraud scheme.
newsitem.headline: N.J. investment adviser charged in fraud scheme.

text.p: A Tenafly, N.J., investment adviser was charged Tuesday with fraud for allegedly bilking clients who entrusted her with over $120 million in investment funds, the U.S. attorney's office for Manhattan said.

Charged with three counts of mail fraud in federal court in Manhattan was Teresa Fernandez, 49, who was president and owner of an investment advisory firm, Wharton Investments Inc, which she operated from her home, prosecutors said.
In the criminal complaint, Fernandez allegedly opened three trading accounts at Bear Stearns Cos Inc for her clients, mostly wealthy residents from the Philippines.

The clients entrusted more than $120 million to her between 1990 and 1995, with one unidentified Filipino investor giving her more than $50 million to invest through two of the three accounts, court papers showed.
In mid-June 1990, Fernandez allegedly sent Bear Stearns a forged letter directing the broker to send duplicate account statements to a Philippine address -- her mother's home.

In a separate civil complaint, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission also charged Fernandez with fraud for allegedly misappropriating $64 million in client funds by forging broker account statements and falsifying instructions to brokers.

Simultaneous with the filing of the SEC complaint, Fernandez settled without admitting or denying guilt, by promising not to further violate federal securities laws. The The SEC is still seeking an order for her to return illegal gains and to pay civil fines.
Fernandez could not be reached for comment.
From that time on, Fernandez allegedly sent her clients fake brokerage statements reporting sham securities trades.

She allegedly opened, without authority from clients, accounts at the Bank of New York Co Inc and then caused Bear Stearns to transfer $61.4 million from the brokerage to the bank, allegedly forging authorization letters from the clients.

Later, she allegedly sent bogus Bear Stearns account statements to the business address of the three accounts in Hong Kong that hid the wire transfers, concealed big trading losses and showed profitable ones -- enough for her to claim more than $5 million in management fees, the complaint said.
As a result, the three accounts allegedly lost about $65 million, the court papers showed.
